reference.source: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Hemangiomas and Malformations
clinicalPearls: Slow-flow malformation of dysplastic lymphatic channels, classified as macrocystic, microcystic or combined.
Macrocystic lesions are soft, transilluminant and often cervicofacial or axillary (historically termed cystic hygroma); microcystic lesions are ill-defined and infiltrative.
Somatic activating PIK3CA mutations underlie most lesions, placing them within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum.
Sudden enlargement typically follows intralesional bleeding or infection.
Superficial microcystic mucosal or cutaneous lesions produce characteristic clear or blood-filled vesicles resembling frogspawn.
Sclerotherapy is first-line for macrocystic disease; microcystic disease is harder to treat and sirolimus is increasingly used.
Large cervicofacial lesions can compromise the airway and may require antenatal airway planning such as an EXIT procedure.
Antenatally detected cystic hygroma is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner syndrome and with other structural anomalies.
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphatic malformation results from abnormal embryonic development of lymphatic channels that fail to establish normal connections with the venous system, producing dilated, endothelium-lined cystic spaces filled with lymph. Most sporadic lesions carry somatic activating mutations in PIK3CA, driving PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and abnormal lymphatic endothelial growth. Because the channels drain poorly they are prone to stasis, intralesional haemorrhage and infection, which cause abrupt and sometimes dramatic enlargement.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroglossal or branchial cyst for cervical lesions
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound distinguishing macrocystic from microcystic disease
Contrast-enhanced MRI (T2-bright cysts with fluid-fluid levels after bleeding)
Antenatal ultrasound and, where indicated, fetal karyotyping
Aspiration and analysis of cyst fluid when the diagnosis is unclear
Airway assessment with nasendoscopy or imaging for cervicofacial lesions
redFlags: Airway compromise from a cervicofacial lesion
Rapid enlargement from intralesional haemorrhage or infection
Sepsis arising within an infected malformation
Chylous effusions or generalised lymphatic anomaly
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on site and type. Well-defined macrocystic lesions respond well to sclerotherapy, whereas diffuse microcystic and cervicofacial disease tends to recur and cause chronic morbidity, although mTOR inhibition has improved control.
pitfalls: Attributing sudden swelling to malignancy rather than to bleeding or infection.
Expecting sclerotherapy to be as effective for microcystic as for macrocystic disease.
Overlooking airway planning in a large antenatally detected cervical lesion.
references: Consensus guidance on management of lymphatic malformations
